title: The Brutal History of The First Warplanes
dek: At the start of World War I, aircraft were dismissed as a joke by the officer class; within four years, the sky had become a meat grinder of reconnaissance, bombing, and dogfighting, where the average life expectancy of a new pilot in 1917 was about two weeks.
why: Joshua Levine uses diaries and archives to make the evolution of air combat from child's play to industrial meat grinder vividly concrete; his mid-to-late analysis of why aces broke their own rules and died is especially rare.
who: Defense and hard-tech investors, founders studying the pace of technology iteration, and team leaders trying to understand why top talent self-destructs.
skip: Channel promos and ad breaks can be skipped; the main content has almost no filler.

points.h: Britain's first plane came from a Wild West showman
points.body: At the start of the war, senior officers still saw cavalry as the main reconnaissance arm and were both snobbish and impatient toward aircraft: airships were treated as a gentleman's mode of transport, while heavier-than-air machines were dirty, noisy, and required mechanics, dismissed as something 'not for our kind of people.' Britain's first plane came from an American, Samuel Cody, who had originally come to Britain with a Wild West show, posing as Buffalo Bill's cousin and performing tricks like shooting eggs off his wife's head before turning to flight. His large aircraft was nicknamed the 'flying birdcage' because it was big enough to hold a canary. Cody later died in a flying accident, which was the norm in early aviation.

points.h: The commander-in-chief only cared if it was cold up there, not about intelligence
points.body: The Royal Flying Corps' initial task was to reconnoiter German movements over France, but the start was almost farcical: two pilots both got lost; one landed and was nearly captured, then was recognized and taken to dinner by the mayor; the other was so disoriented that he flew over a large city before realizing it was Brussels. Yet they soon began reporting genuinely useful intelligence. One pilot sketched what he saw on his knee board and reported back to Sir John French, but French was not interested in the intelligence—he only asked whether it was cold up there and how far one could see. French's skepticism later proved completely wrong, and only then were aircraft taken seriously step by step.

points.h: Aircraft changed war with eyes, not machine guns
points.body: The most critical air achievement of WWI was not shooting down but seeing. On September 13, observer Atkinson's report twice noted 'trenches are being dug in the fields.' Joshua says this was the beginning of everything—from then on the Western Front entered trench warfare, and reconnaissance aircraft went from dispensable novelties to truly essential eyes and ears. Later that same day, Sir John French officially issued a commendation to the flying corps. In other words, aircraft changed war not because of machine guns but because they were the only eyes that could see the whole battlefield.

points.h: Bombing was not designed by generals but tried out by pilots
points.body: Bombing and air combat were not designed by generals but tried out by pilots themselves. Initially they dropped steel darts from planes, then hand grenades, and only later strapped on bombs. One pilot cut a hole in the bottom of his fuselage and lined it with tin to form a chute for dropping bombs, but the airflow compressed the tin and jammed the bomb, leaving the detonator exposed beneath the belly. He passed a note to Louis Strange saying, 'We are going to die.' The two chose to land and wait for the explosion, but the tall corn in the field pulled the detonator off, and they emerged unscathed. Louis Strange later died peacefully in bed at an old age—that was the daily reality of early flying.

points.h: One mechanical device made every Allied aircraft obsolete overnight
points.body: To fire a machine gun forward through the propeller, the Dutchman Fokker first offered the solution to the Allies; they declined, so he turned to building aircraft for Germany. His mechanical device allowed bullets to fire only in the gaps between propeller blades, suddenly enabling German pilots to aim head-on, making all existing Allied aircraft instantly obsolete—'going up meant going to die.' This moment is comparable to how drones on today's Ukrainian front become obsolete within weeks of arrival—WWI air combat was itself an arms race measured in months, even weeks.

points.h: Average life of two weeks, yet with orderlies and a roller rink
points.body: Fighter pilots lived a life of extremes. During the 1917 Battle of Arras, the average time from a new pilot's arrival at the front to death was only about two weeks; many were sent into battle with severely inadequate training, and conditions like 'flying sickness'—a mental breakdown treated with more leniency—appeared. Yet at the same time, they were housed behind the front lines, with orderlies, could go into town for drinks, had favorite restaurants, and one squadron commander even poured concrete himself to build a roller rink. Comfort and terror coexisted—that was the daily life of a fighter pilot.

points.h: Too-famous aces may have actively chosen when to die
points.body: Both Richthofen and McCudden wrote down their own air combat rules, such as 'after shooting down an enemy, do not follow him down over his own lines,' because low altitude made you a target for ground rifles and machine guns. Yet these two most elite and symbolic pilots ultimately died precisely by violating their own rules. Joshua does not accept the explanation that 'they thought they were above the rules,' and offers another possibility: because they were so famous, they were kept continuously at the front, and subconsciously knew they would die sooner or later, so they chose to end it at a time and place they could control, rather than wait for the enemy to choose.
